cells.tense: You are the one deciding what's worth holding onto from what just changed, and you are doing it on purpose.
cells.ask: Write down the two things from the last big change you're holding onto, and one you're handing to someone else this week.
cells.core:
Something arrived this season and you were ready for it. You've been sorting what to hold onto and what to let pass, and you're doing it on purpose, not out of fear. That's the calm part — you know the difference between keeping something safe and refusing to move on.
What you're holding onto finds its way to people who need it, and what you need back usually finds its way to you. That exchange is the quiet engine here. It isn't fragile. It can take one more thing being given away, or one more thing being asked for, without you losing your footing. That's the balance worth keeping — not stillness. Just even movement.

cells.tense: You are bracing for something that has not arrived yet, and the bracing has become the whole job.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're holding 'just in case' and put it back in the world — give it, lend it, or tell someone what it's for.
cells.core:
You're guarding a door nothing has knocked on yet. Your grip has gotten tighter than the thing in it needs, and some of the energy in that grip is going toward futures that may not show up. That's not wrong — it means you care. But the grip is starting to feel like the point.
Some of what you're holding onto isn't yours to hand down, and it won't be needed the way you think. You can loosen one thing without losing the ground under you. Not all of it. One. Let it move back into the room it came from, and notice whether the door still stands.

cells.tense: You stopped standing at that door and part of you is still waiting on the other side of it.
cells.ask: Name one thing you meant to hold onto from the last change and put it where it lives — a shelf, a file, a person who should have it.
cells.core:
You went through something and then just kept walking. Not much got held onto — what mattered got left where it fell, and you've been looking back at the door instead of forward at what you're carrying. It's not that you don't care. It's that the caring went quiet.
What's coming toward you now needs a place to land, and the landing spot is hollow. Not the whole floor — just that one spot. Put one thing that mattered where it actually belongs. Not into storage, not into a someday pile. Somewhere you'll see it, or someone who should have it. The ground under you is already there. You just haven't set anything down on it.

cells.tense: You are already holding the shape of what just arrived, and you are explaining it as if it were the weather.
cells.ask: Say out loud, once, that you kept one thing from the last change on purpose — then put it where you'll actually use it.
cells.core:
You're holding onto something from the last change quietly, without making a thing of it, and when you talk about it, it comes out as circumstance. As if it happened on its own and you just happened to be there. Your choice is real. It's being filed under 'that's how it went.'
That's the leak. Not that you're doing it wrong, but that the decision isn't being claimed. This doesn't call for more effort — it calls for one sentence, in your own voice, to one person. Then put the thing down where it belongs and let it be seen there. That's the whole move.
